items.stem: Use the foreign-exchange model in which net capital outflow determines a vertical supply curve for domestic currency. A tariff and capital flight occur together. At the original exchange rate, the tariff increases currency demand by 40 units. After interest rates adjust, the final increase in net capital outflow adds 65 units to currency supply. Prices and other factors affecting demand stay fixed. What happens to the exchange rate and net exports, and what more would we need to know to calculate the size of the exchange-rate change?
options: The currency appreciates and NX rises 40 units; the slope of the supply curve for loanable funds alone measures appreciation
The currency depreciates and NX rises 65 units; the NX-demand slope is needed to quantify depreciation
The currency depreciates but NX is unchanged; tariffs fix the trade balance
The rate is unchanged and NX rises 105 units; horizontal shifts can simply be added
items.feedback: At the old rate, supply rises 25 units more than demand, creating excess supply. The foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency quote falls until demand matches final NCO. NX rises 65 by identity; the remaining exchange-rate change requires the NX-demand response.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Group the model assumptions and the two numerical shifts; explain NX-demand slope in natural terms while preserving the magnitude-versus-direction distinction.

items.stem: A lab chooses Compound A, which uses its entire allocation of 12 scientist-months and 5 sequencer slots. Instead, Platform B would use all 12 months and 5 slots for $11 million net value. Three smaller projects each need 6 scientist-months: C uses 3 slots and yields $8 million before $2 million in new costs; D uses 2 slots and yields $7 million before $2 million in new costs; E uses 3 slots and yields $10 million before $2 million in new costs. Projects are indivisible, compatible if both resource limits are met, and their net values add. What is the opportunity cost of assigning the resources to Compound A?
options: $13 million: the net value of projects D and E.
$14 million: the net value of projects C and E.
$11 million: the net value of the full Platform B.
$17 million: the gross value of projects D and E.
items.feedback: Net values are C = $6m, D = $5m and E = $8m. D plus E uses 12 scientist-months and 5 slots and yields $13m. C plus E would yield $14m but needs 6 slots, so it is infeasible. C plus D and Platform B each yield $11m. The best feasible alternative forgone is therefore D plus E, worth $13m net.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: The substantive resource-allocation problem is good. Put alternatives, resource use, gross/net values and costs into a table with a short prose introduction.

items.stem: A studio selects a film that uses both of its release slots and all 8 available editor-weeks. Its alternatives are indivisible. A documentary uses 1 slot and 3 editor-weeks for $6 million net return. A series uses 1 slot and 5 editor-weeks for $9 million net return. A concert uses 1 slot and 4 editor-weeks, earning $12 million before $2 million of new costs. A festival package uses both slots and 8 editor-weeks for $14 million net return. Projects can be combined when both capacity limits are met, and net returns add. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting the film?
options: The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
The series and concert, with $19 million net return.
The documentary and series, with $15 million net return.
The festival package alone, with $14 million net return.
items.feedback: The concert nets $10m. Combining it with the documentary yields $16m and uses 2 slots and 7 editor-weeks. The series plus concert would yield $19m but requires 9 editor-weeks, so it is infeasible. The documentary plus series yields $15m, and the festival package yields $14m. The best feasible use forgone is the $16m documentary-concert bundle.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite

items.stem: Maintenance uses a weekend that could otherwise produce a certain $40,000 net value. Before the decision, an urgent order becomes available: a 50% chance of $80,000 net value and a 50% chance of zero; it cannot be combined with the regular order. A guarantee costing $6,000 would make the urgent order’s $80,000 certain. For a risk-neutral manager, what is the opportunity cost of maintenance?

$40,000: the original plan fixes opportunity cost even after a better alternative becomes feasible.
$80,000: use the guaranteed receipt while ignoring the resources needed to obtain the guarantee.
items.feedback: The regular and unguaranteed urgent orders each have expected net value 40,000. The guaranteed order nets 80,000-6,000=74,000 and is feasible before maintenance is chosen. Mutually exclusive alternatives are compared, not added.

decision.note: The alternatives, probability, guarantee cost and risk-neutral assumption are clearly connected.

items.stem: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds the inflation effect of the supply disruption ending.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above the original curve; its position relative to the curve during the disruption depends on the sizes of the two effects.
items.feedback: Neither the supply disruption nor the higher expected inflation affected the original curve. The final curve reflects only the higher expected inflation, so it remains above the original curve. Comparing the final curve with the curve during the disruption requires comparing the sizes of those two effects; observed inflation alone does not establish them.

decision.note: The longer setup is warranted to distinguish a temporary supply disruption from lasting expectation changes.

Inflexible users must stop consuming before the price difference can affect peak demand.
Flexible users shift some use overnight, reducing peak pressure without requiring every household to shift.
All households must use less electricity over the full day for timing prices to reduce peak demand.
items.feedback: Higher peak prices encourage users with flexible timing to move consumption. Daily consumption need not fall, and users with urgent needs need not shift for this coordinating effect to occur.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: One straightforward application of peak pricing; naturally written.

items.stem: A factory raises both outputs after reorganizing idle workers. Later, training expands the maximum output possible even when all workers are occupied. Which evidence separates the two improvements?
options: The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
Any simultaneous output increase proves the frontier shifted
Any training program moves production along an unchanged frontier
Both improvements establish that the original output was outside the frontier
items.feedback: Using idle resources can raise both outputs without changing capacity. A higher maximum under full efficient use establishes a frontier expansion.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Classifying an efficiency improvement versus capacity growth is a routine two-example distinction.

items.stem: A plant initially produces 24,000 units using 20 workers who each work 100 hours. Next period, 24 workers each work 80 hours and produce 25,344 units. Which comparison is correct?
options: Output per worker falls 12%; output per hour rises 10%
Both productivity measures rise 5.6%, matching total output
Output per worker rises 10%; output per hour falls 12%
Output per hour is unchanged because the plant hired more workers
items.feedback: Per-worker output falls from 1,200 to 1,056, or 12%. Total hours fall from 2,000 to 1,920; hourly output rises from 12 to 13.2, or 10%. Changes in hours per worker make the productivity measures diverge.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Clear two-denominator productivity calculation; concise answer comparisons.

items.stem: An economy initially produces $90 billion using 3 billion labor hours. A plan targets $108 billion while limiting total hours to 3.2 billion. What hourly productivity and increase over the initial level are required?
options: $33.75 per hour, a 12.5% increase
$36 per hour, a 20% increase
$30 per hour, with no productivity gain
$28.125 per hour, a 6.25% decline
items.feedback: Initial productivity is 90/3 = 30 dollars per hour. The target requires 108/3.2 = 33.75, or 12.5% more. Output growth alone overstates the needed productivity increase because hours also expand.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Clear target productivity and percentage-increase calculation.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. An analyst describes the move from a to b as a rightward shift of money demand and says that doubling the money quantity proves a doubling of the price level. Is the analyst’s conclusion correct?
options: MD is unchanged; the price level rises by one-third, so constant output would require velocity to fall.
MD shifts right; the price level doubles, so velocity can remain fixed.
MD is unchanged; the price level falls by one-quarter, so velocity must rise.
MD shifts left; the price level is unchanged because the money supply is vertical.
items.feedback: The same MD contains both a and b. Money doubles from 2,500 to 5,000, while P rises from 1/2 to 2/3, a factor of 4/3. With Y fixed, MV = PY requires velocity to change by (4/3)/2 = 2/3, so it falls.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Write the money-demand curve is unchanged instead of the MD label; retain the graph-based quantity/price/velocity reasoning.

items.stem: Use MV=PY. In period 1, independently verified money is 200, velocity is 5, and real output is 500; the reported price index is 2.4. In period 2, money rises 20% and velocity falls 10%. Independently verified nominal spending is 1,080 and the price index is 2.16, while reported real output is 600. Which corrections reconcile both periods, and what is the corrected inflation rate?
options: Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: 8%.
Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 600; inflation: 8%.
Period-1 price index: 2.4; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: −10%.
Period-1 price index: 2; period-2 real output: 500; inflation: 10%.
items.feedback: Period 1 gives P=200×5/500=2. Period 2 gives M=240 and V=4.5, so MV=1,080, agreeing with independently measured spending. Its verified P=2.16 requires Y=1,080/2.16=500. Corrected inflation is 2.16/2−1=8%; using the erroneous first price index would give a false decline.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: Separate verified versus reported values in a two-period table; present corrected results in parallel sentences or table columns.

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power
items.stem: Relative PPP predicts depreciation of a domestic currency, but it depreciates less over the observed interval. The report gives no horizon or evidence about traded-goods price gaps. Which follow-up best distinguishes short-run deviation from persistent limits to PPP?
options: Replace the nominal quote with its reciprocal and treat the discrepancy as resolved
Examine the horizon and whether gaps are concentrated in nontraded or costly-to-arbitrage goods
Infer that inflation data are wrong because depreciation differed from the benchmark
Infer that capital flows cannot matter because PPP already predicts a direction
items.feedback: A short interval can reflect asset-demand or policy forces, while persistent nontradable or trade-cost gaps can limit arbitrage. The discrepancy alone identifies neither measurement error nor the source and persistence of the deviation.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Horizon and costly-to-arbitrage goods are terse; ask about the time span and barriers to trading goods across borders.

items.stem: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
items.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: A number followed by one clear economic interpretation is concise and readable.

items.stem: Initially 160 books cost $4 each and 80 meals cost $10 each. Both quantities rise 10% and both prices 20%, so nominal GDP rises 32%. An analyst says using different positive base prices could change real growth from 10% to 32%. Is that possible here?
options: Yes. Choosing current prices as fixed weights always turns nominal growth into real growth.
No. Because both quantities rise by the same 10%, any fixed positive price weights give 10% real growth;32% includes price growth.
No. Real growth is 12% under every weighting because 32 minus 20 is exact deflation.
Yes. A higher weight on either good changes its quantity growth from 10% to 32%.
items.feedback: With uniform quantity growth, the whole fixed-price sum is multiplied by 1.10 regardless of the chosen positive weights. Nominal growth is 1.10×1.20−1=32%. This weight-invariance depends on uniform quantity growth; it is not a general rule for changing output composition.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Insert the missing space in growth;32%. The substance and complete-sentence prose are otherwise sound.

items.stem: A person earns 8% nominal interest on savings, faces 6% inflation and receives a 4% wage increase. They claim their overall purchasing power must have risen because the savings return is positive in real terms. Is that conclusion established?
options: No. Real savings returns rise and real wages fall; their amounts determine the combined effect.
Yes. A positive real savings return ensures that total purchasing power rises despite falling real wages.
No. Both real savings returns and real wages fall whenever inflation is positive.
Yes. Add the 8% interest rate and 4% wage increase, then subtract 6% inflation.
items.feedback: The savings return exceeds inflation, while wage growth falls short of it. Combining those effects requires their economic weights; adding percentage changes on different bases cannot establish an overall purchasing-power gain.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: Positive real savings returns are not the same as real savings returns rise. No earlier return is given; describe the positive real return and falling real wage without claiming a rate increase.

items.stem: A disinflation lowers inflation from 10 percent to 6 percent. Cumulative output loss is 18 percent of one year’s potential GDP, of which 11 percent occurred before the final year. An analyst reports a sacrifice ratio using only the final-year loss. Which audit correction is needed?
options: Use all 18 percent: the ratio is 4.5; using only the final year would understate it as 1.75.
Use only 7 percent: the ratio is 1.75 because earlier output losses are already over.
Use the final inflation rate: the ratio is 3 because the target is 6 percent.
Add initial and final inflation: the ratio is 1.125 because the full window contains both rates.
items.feedback: The inflation reduction is 4 percentage points. Cumulative loss gives 18/4 = 4.5. Final-year loss is 18 − 11 = 7, giving 7/4 = 1.75 if earlier losses are wrongly omitted. Returning toward potential does not erase earlier lost production.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Which audit correction is needed can directly ask how the sacrifice ratio should be calculated.

items.stem: Policymakers planned to reduce inflation by 3 percentage points at a sacrifice ratio of 2, accepting a maximum cumulative output loss of 6%. The first percentage-point reduction unexpectedly costs 4% of annual output. If each further percentage-point reduction costs 2% of annual output, how much further can inflation fall within the loss limit, and what would achieving the original target cost?
options: No further point can be achieved because the first loss exceeded its forecast
The target can increase because a larger first loss lowers all later losses mechanically
Only one further point fits within the additional 2% output loss permitted; achieving all 3 points would require total loss 8%
All remaining 2 points fit because the original average ratio remains 2 by assumption
items.feedback: The remaining permitted loss is 6% − 4% = 2%. At an output cost of 2% per percentage point, inflation can fall by one more percentage point. Completing the original target would require two more percentage points, costing another 4% of output for a total loss of 8%.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: The correct answer covers both remaining reduction and full-target cost; make all options answer both parts in similarly clear terms.

items.stem: In a closed economy, output is $1,240 billion, consumption is $790 billion and government purchases are $230 billion. Firms planned $250 billion of investment, including planned inventory accumulation. Output and final purchases are realized as stated. What are realized saving and investment, including the unplanned inventory change?
options: $220 billion of saving and $250 billion of realized investment, leaving a $30 billion accounting gap
$220 billion of realized saving and investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory reduction
$250 billion of realized saving and investment, with consumption automatically $30 billion lower
$220 billion of realized investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory increase
items.feedback: Realized saving is Y − C − G = 1,240 − 790 − 230 = $220 billion. Realized investment includes inventories, so it is also $220 billion. Relative to planned investment of $250 billion, unplanned inventory investment is −$30 billion. Equality of realized aggregates does not require equality of plans at every interest rate.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The planned/realised accounting distinction is explicit and readable.

items.stem: Following an earthquake, a hospital has one surgical team for trauma cases, routine emergencies, and patients already scheduled. Which policy best acknowledges scarcity without pretending one criterion settles the decision?
options: Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.
Treat trauma first in every case, using the emergency label as sufficient evidence that postponed care has lower marginal value.
Preserve scheduled order in every case, using earlier commitments as sufficient evidence that urgent arrivals have lower priority.
Allocate equal team time to each group, using equal shares as sufficient evidence of both fair treatment and greatest health gain.
items.feedback: The surgical team has competing uses with differences in urgency, benefits and forgone care. No label or equal-time rule settles every dimension without evaluating the feasible alternatives.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Without pretending one criterion settles the decision is author commentary; ask directly how to compare the competing uses of the surgical team.

items.stem: One crew can inspect 18 bridges or repair 6 mains per month at a constant tradeoff. A plan requires at least 6 inspections and proposes 5 main repairs. Extra funding cannot add crew time this month. Which revision is feasible, and what does the limit show?
options: Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 4; money alone does not supply the missing crew capacity.
Keep 6 inspections and 5 repairs; separate maximum outputs can be combined without sacrificing either.
Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 2; one repair displaces six bridge inspections.
Cancel every main repair; any minimum inspection requirement uses the crew’s entire monthly capacity.
items.feedback: Each main repair costs 18/6=3 inspections. Six inspections use one-third of capacity, leaving two-thirds for 4 repairs. The proposed 6/18+5/6=7/6 of a crew-month is infeasible even with enough funding.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Clear capacity constraint, feasible revision and distinction between funding and real resources.

items.stem: Productivity rises permanently, expected prices rise, and oil prices fall. What is the most accurate result?
options: Higher expected prices lower LRAS; productivity and cheaper oil raise SRAS, so the curves move in opposite directions
Productivity leaves LRAS fixed; expected prices and cheaper oil offset in SRAS, so both curves remain unchanged
Productivity raises LRAS; higher expected prices oppose productivity and cheaper oil in SRAS, so its net direction is uncertain
Productivity raises LRAS; expected prices and cheaper oil reinforce productivity in SRAS, so both curves shift right
items.feedback: Productivity raises capacity; expected prices and oil prices push SRAS in opposite directions.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: Productivity raises LRAS and effects oppose ... in SRAS are compressed model notes. Ask which curves shift and explain the competing short-run effects in sentences.

items.stem: Later observations put unemployment at the rate shown at A, but inflation stays above A's level. Which evidence would support a higher short-run Phillips curve crossing the same LRPC, rather than a vertical short-run curve?
options: Unemployment remains 2.5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
Unemployment remains 5%, and a higher price level alone proves the short-run curve has become vertical.
Unemployment remains 5%, and unchanged expectations explain a lasting upward SRPC shift with no other supply change.
Unemployment remains 5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
items.feedback: A is at unemployment 5% and inflation 2.5%. Higher expected inflation can raise SRPC while the same natural rate preserves LRPC. An observed price level or unchanged unemployment alone does not establish that expectations have adjusted.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The conditional graph/expectation comparison is demanding but clear.

items.stem: A plant buys new machines but lacks workers trained to operate them. One proposal subsidizes machines alone; another subsidizes machines and worker training. Why might the first proposal produce a smaller productivity gain?
options: Physical capital needs complementary skills; pairing training can make the machines more productive.
Physical capital replaces all skills; training cannot alter the machines' contribution to output.
Training replaces all machines; purchasing equipment cannot contribute to output after training.
The two proposals are identical; both add only to the physical capital stock.
items.feedback: New machines add physical capital, while training adds human capital. Complementarity means a shortage of operational skills can prevent machines from realizing their productive potential; the combined proposal addresses that constraint.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Pairing training is awkward. The task is simple complementarity recognition and the alternatives are extreme.

items.stem: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
options: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
Automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn; the delayed program may add demand after recovery.
Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
items.feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap. Automatic stabilizers recede as the economy recovers.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The timing comparison is expressed in a concrete, natural scenario.

items.stem: A recessionary output gap is $240. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $60 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
options: The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
items.feedback: The current calculation is 4×60=240. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The spending calculation is already supplied, leaving the timing caveat. Compare with items 91 and 167 before retaining multiple similar Legendary variants.

items.stem: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 70 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
items.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: Support/restraint labels do not identify policy actions or the short-run comparison clearly. Spell out expansionary and contractionary demand policy and their tradeoffs.

items.stem: Labor demand is Ld=120-2Wf and supply is Ls=2Ww. Wf is the employer’s total cost and Ww is take-home pay. An $8 per-worker payroll tax is legally moved from firms to workers without other changes. Which prediction refutes the claim that firms’ economic burden disappears?
options: Wf falls to $30 and Ww to $22, with employment 60; legal reassignment removes all employer burden.
Wf remains $34 and Ww rises to $34, with employment 52; workers now remit the tax from a higher net wage.
Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
Wf rises to $38 and Ww stays $30, with employment 44; firms bear all tax whenever labor demand slopes down.
items.feedback: The wedge is Wf-Ww=8 regardless of remitter. Solve 120-2(Ww+8)=2Ww: Ww=26, Wf=34 and L=52. Without tax W=30. Employer and worker burdens are 4 each, unchanged by the statutory relabeling.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Symbols are defined, and each answer connects numerical results to economic incidence in a readable sentence.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. A technology improvement shifts supply from S0 to S1. At the unchanged price of $3, quantity supplied rises. Half of this increase in quantity is later lost, leaving a parallel supply curve halfway between S0 and S1. What price would now be needed to supply the quantity originally available on S1 at $3, and how would the market reach that quantity?
options: About $2.50; movement down the halfway curve offsets the lost capacity.
About $3.00; unchanged desired output prevents a supply shift.
About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
About $4.00; movement up S0 offsets the entire improvement.
items.feedback: At $3, S0 supplies about 100 thousand and S1 about 225 thousand. The halfway curve supplies about 162.5 thousand at $3. At 225 thousand, S0 requires $4 and S1 $3, so the halfway curve requires $3.50. A price movement along that new curve restores quantity; it does not undo the partial technology loss.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The graph counterfactual and halfway shift are fully described without unnecessary template language.

items.stem: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?
options: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls
items.feedback: The vertical supply curve holds quantity at 200. Buyers pay the same demand price at that quantity, so sellers absorb the full $6 wedge through lower net receipts. Revenue is $1,200. With no trades lost and no other distortions in the stated model, tax revenue is a transfer and there is no deadweight loss.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: Three connected results are expressed as a complete sentence; no rewrite solely for listing three outputs.

items.stem: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
options: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.
items.feedback: Compare absolute elasticities. Initially 0.25 1.20, so sellers are relatively less responsive. Greater demand responsiveness also increases the quantity response to a comparable small tax.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The elasticity comparison and its incidence/quantity implications are clear.

items.stem: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A review finds that CS plus PS falls by $480,000 after the displayed tax. With no externalities or collection costs, how should that change be reconciled with incidence and total surplus?
options: $480,000 is lost surplus, while the $400,000 revenue is an additional loss
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and each side bears $2 per unit
$560,000 becomes revenue, total surplus rises $80,000, and each side bears $2
$400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and buyers bear all $4 per unit
items.feedback: Read the old price $12, buyer price $14, seller receipt $10 and taxed quantity 100,000. The $4 wedge raises $400,000. Subtracting that transfer from the $480,000 private loss leaves $80,000 of lost surplus, also 0.5 × 40,000 × $4. Each side bears $2 on each remaining unit.

decision.label: Light edit
decision.note: Reconciled with incidence and total surplus can become a direct question about transfers, lost surplus and the tax burden.

items.stem: In Year 1, employed = 150 million, unemployed = 10 million, and not in labor force = 90 million. In Year 2, employed = 152 million, unemployed = 8 million, and not in labor force = 95 million. What is the best interpretation?
options: Employment rose, unemployment rose, and labor-force participation rose
Employment fell because not-in-labor-force increased
Employment rose, the unemployment rate fell, but labor-force participation fell
The unemployment rate stayed constant because the labor force stayed at 160 million
items.feedback: Employment rises from 150 to 152. The unemployment rate falls from 10/160 to 8/160. But participation falls because adult population rises while the labor force stays at 160.

decision.label: Prose/layout rewrite
decision.note: Two years of employed = ... data should be a small table followed by a direct comparison question; answer wording is already clear.

items.stem: Demand is at its normal level. Each week, 40 qualified workers start searching for suitable existing vacancies. Average search lasts 6 weeks. A job-information service cuts that duration to 3 weeks without changing entries into search or job requirements. Another 180 job seekers lack the skills vacancies require. Assume steady flows, so the frictionally unemployed equal weekly entries times average search duration. What does the service change, and what would address the remaining mismatch?
options: Frictional unemployment falls by 240; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; the information service also removes all structural unemployment without retraining.
Frictional unemployment falls by 120; retraining addresses the 180 mismatched workers, while demand stimulus alone need not do so.
Frictional unemployment stays unchanged; only stronger aggregate demand can shorten search when suitable vacancies already exist.
items.feedback: The steady search stock falls from 40×6=240 to 40×3=120. Better information reduces search time and frictional unemployment. It does not supply missing skills, so the separate structural mismatch calls for a skill response. At normal demand, an aggregate-demand increase is not a substitute for these targeted changes.

decision.label: Keep wording
decision.note: The longer explanation makes the steady-flow calculation self-contained and connects it to a different unemployment mechanism.

limitations: This is a full-bank automated wording screen plus a 176-item qualitative audit, not a line-by-line editorial review of all 1,360 questions.
The sample intentionally covers every topic and adds high-indicator cases; sample percentages are not estimates of whole-bank prevalence.
Equations, abbreviations, semicolons and short numeric answer pairs are not automatically defects.
Difficulty, distractor and assumption flags request follow-up; they do not authorise tier moves or establish that all answer keys are correct.
Explanations and graphs were consulted selectively; this is not a complete mathematical or graphical revalidation.
